Executive Summary

Project Chunker represents a foundational paradigm shift in software repository lifecycle management, deterministic snapshotting, and atomic filesystem archiving. Engineered specifically for lightweight POSIX and mobile Linux environments (most notably Android Termux on ARM64), it eliminates the runtime baggage of traditional external relational databases and cloud object stores. By consolidating entire directory structures, text sources, binary assets, and metadata trackers into single-file BEJSON 104a containers, Project Chunker provides bit-for-bit verifiability, zero-risk atomic archive-and-wipe (“scoop”) mechanics, and automated package version tracking. This comprehensive architectural manual examines the low-level protocols, data schemas, verification engines, and operational workflows that power the system.

1. The Architectural Imperative of Local-First, Zero-SQL Archiving

1.1 Limitations of Monolithic VCS and Database Engines on Constrained POSIX Runtimes

Modern software engineering has increasingly centralized repository lifecycle tracking around external relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL), hosted cloud object storage systems (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage), and distributed version control systems (Git). While these enterprise tools excel across distributed teams operating on gigabit fiber connections and multi-core servers, they become brittle, bloated, and vulnerable when deployed inside constrained, single-user mobile Linux environments—most notably Android Termux on ARM64.

On mobile devices, running persistent database daemon servers (like mysqld or postgres) introduces immense memory pressure, socket permission barriers, and aggressive termination by the Android Low-Memory Killer (LMK). Furthermore, monolithic .git repository trees accumulate hundreds of loose object files, lock contention issues during battery-saver throttling, and complex index corruption when processes are halted abruptly. When an engineer or autonomous coding assistant must package, archive, inspect, and relocate complete project trees across local storage, external SD cards, and download folders, reliance on external daemons inevitably introduces downtime and data loss.

In contrast, local developers and autonomous agent loops require deterministic operations that satisfy four core criteria: zero initialization latency, atomic write resilience against sudden process termination, bit-for-bit mathematical repeatability, and complete elimination of unmanaged disk clutter. Standard archive utilities (such as tarballs and plain zip files) partially address storage consolidation, but they lack schema-governed metadata, unified version tracking, cryptographic integrity audits, and safe bi-directional deployment pipelines.

1.2 The Local-First Zero-SQL Philosophy: Self-Contained Persistence

Project Chunker was designed to completely bypass these architectural vulnerabilities through the Local-First, Zero-SQL architectural paradigm. Under this design pattern, every database table, project manifest, file chunk, and execution log is persisted directly within the filesystem as a human-readable, deterministic BEJSON 104a document.

The foundational tenets of Project Chunker are:

  • Zero External Daemon Dependencies: The entire storage engine operates through standard POSIX file operations using pure Python standard library modules (json, hashlib, base64, shutil, os, pathlib). No background database processes, socket servers, or port allocations are required for data persistence.
  • Single-File Containerization: An entire project directory containing hundreds of nested source code files, documentation, binary graphics, and configuration files is consolidated into a single, flat .bejson text snapshot file. This eliminates filesystem bloat and inode exhaustion.
  • Immutable Cryptographic Verification: Every file record within a snapshot encapsulates a streaming SHA-256 cryptographic digest. Once serialized, a snapshot is immutable; any modification or bit rot is detectable upon ingestion.
  • Total Portability: A single snapshot file contains 100% of the payload and metadata required to re-instantiate the project on any POSIX-compliant system without external network access.

1.3 BEJSON 104a Core Standard & Policy §6.2 O(1) Field Map Caching Compliance

Standard JSON structures repeat object keys across every record in a collection, wasting massive amounts of storage space and inflating token usage during LLM interactions. The BEJSON 104a format resolves this by strictly decoupling schema metadata from relational rows:

Structural Header Data Type Architectural Purpose
Format string Identifies specification family; strictly "BEJSON".
Format_Version string Designates specification generation; strictly "104a".
Records_Type array[string] Declares entity classifications contained within the table (e.g. ["SnapshotEntity"]).
Fields array[object] Ordered array of column specifications: {"name": "...", "type": "..."}.
Values array[array] Two-dimensional positional value matrix strictly matching the positional offsets of Fields.

To prevent brittle positional bugs where code crashes if columns are re-ordered or expanded, Policy §6.2 strictly mandates the use of an O(1) Field Map Cache: 

def process_bejson_records(bejson_document: dict):
    # Mandatory Policy §6.2: Build O(1) Field Map Cache dictionary
    fields_array = bejson_document.get("Fields", [])
    field_map_cache = {field_obj["name"]: col_idx for col_idx, field_obj in enumerate(fields_array)}

    # Extract required indices safely without hardcoding integers
    rel_path_idx = field_map_cache.get("Relative_Path")
    file_hash_idx = field_map_cache.get("File_Hash")
    is_binary_idx = field_map_cache.get("Is_Binary")

    for record_row in bejson_document.get("Values", []):
        target_path = record_row[rel_path_idx]
        expected_hash = record_row[file_hash_idx]
        # Positional access is fully guarded and O(1) compliant
        print(f"Verified: {target_path} -> {expected_hash}")

2. The 3 Data Pillars: In-Depth Schema Specifications & Dual-MFDB Topology

Project Chunker implements a decoupled Dual-MFDB (Multi-File Database) topology. Rather than forcing metadata indices, tracker histories, and dense binary snapshots into a single bloated database file, the system partitions state across three distinct, symbiotic data pillars.

2.1 Pillar 1: Master Registry (storage/master/data/registry.bejson)

The Master Registry represents the global index plane of Project Chunker. It records every tracked project version across the filesystem, linking its unique Versioned_UUID to its historical tracker table, original filesystem origin, release status, and package metrics.

Each column in Pillar 1 serves a critical lifecycle function:

  • Versioned_UUID: The immutable foreign key linking the entry to its corresponding row in the historical tracker and snapshot chunk container.
  • Project_Name: The canonical, normalized project name used for categorization and grouping.
  • Project_Version & Package_Version: Application runtime release state paired with the sequential package delivery integer.
  • Tracker_File: Relative path pointing directly to the project's dedicated historical table in Pillar 2.
  • Original_Path: The absolute host filesystem directory where the project originally resided prior to chunking or scooping.
  • Status: Standardized lifecycle token (Active, Inactive, Legacy).

2.2 Pillar 2: Project Tracker Database (storage/trackers/data/<project>.bejson)

To preserve the complete historical evolution of each project without mutating prior records, every unique project receives a dedicated tracker table under storage/trackers/data/. Whenever a project is chunked or scooped, its complete, verbatim bejson_project.json document is captured as an escaped JSON string within Tracker_Data.

3.1 The 4-Tier Identity Resolution Priority Matrix

In practical environments, incoming code drops, download zip archives, and repositories exhibit varying degrees of metadata discipline. Project Chunker resolves this through an authoritative 4-Tier Identity Resolution Engine implemented in lib_bejson_Projects_tracker.py:

3.2 Filesystem Traversal, Boundary Isolation & Exclusion Filtering

Filesystem crawling is performed recursively using os.walk wrapped by lib_bejson_Projects_filters.py. The crawling engine strictly enforces boundary isolation:

  • In-Place Directory Pruning: Excluded folders (e.g. __pycache__, .git, node_modules, .pytest_cache) are deleted in-place from dirnames during the walk, preventing the engine from ever traversing or reading children of excluded paths.
  • Normalized Relative Matching: Path filters containing a slash (such as data/temp/*) are matched against the normalized relative path from the project root rather than basenames.
  • Self-Chunking Recursion Shield: Project Chunker automatically detects if the target directory contains its own storage repository, pruning storage/ to prevent recursive infinite loops.

3.3 64 KB Chunk Streaming & Content-Addressed SHA-256 Hashing

To prevent out-of-memory errors when processing large codebases on mobile devices with constrained RAM budgets, file reading is streamed in binary mode using 64 KB chunks: 

def compute_streaming_file_sha256(absolute_file_path: Path) -> str:
    """Stream file bytes in 64KB blocks to generate authoritative SHA-256."""
    sha256_hasher = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(absolute_file_path, "rb") as file_stream:
        while byte_chunk := file_stream.read(65536):
            sha256_hasher.update(byte_chunk)
    return sha256_hasher.hexdigest()

3.4 Binary Detection, Base64 Encoding & Payload Packing

Files are automatically classified into text or binary payloads using an 8,192-byte inspection heuristic:

  1. The initial 8 KB block is analyzed. If a null byte (b'\x00') is discovered, the file is immediately tagged as binary.
  2. If no null byte is present, the engine attempts to decode the entire block as UTF-8. If a UnicodeDecodeError is raised, it is flagged as binary.
  3. Binary Ingestion (Binary_Enabled=true): The binary payload is encoded via standard Base64: base64.b64encode(raw_bytes).decode('ascii'). File_Content is stored as an empty string, and the Flags array is populated with ["Is_Binary"].
  4. Text Ingestion: The file content is stored directly within File_Content as UTF-8 text, with Base64 remaining an empty string.

3.5 Empty Directory Capture Semantics & Synthetic Entity Management

Standard tar and zip tools frequently discard empty directory structures, causing runtime FileNotFoundError bugs when software assumes staging directories exist on launch. Project Chunker explicitly preserves directory topology:

If a directory contains zero files and zero child folders after applying exclusion filters, an explicit entity row is written to the snapshot with Is_Empty_Dir=true and empty strings for content, base64, and hashes. However, if a directory is empty purely because all its children were excluded (e.g. an isolated __pycache__ folder), the synthetic entry is suppressed.

3.6 Filename Normalization and Automated Version Parsing Regex

When processing raw incoming archive drops from mobile download folders, project packages frequently follow solid numeric naming conventions mandated by Policy §3.1. To automatically extract project names, application runtime versions, and package exchange numbers without requiring manual developer input, Project Chunker implements a high-precision regular expression parser in lib_bejson_Projects_tracker.py: 

import re
from typing import Optional, Tuple

PACKAGE_FILENAME_REGEX = re.compile(
    r"^(?P<name>[A-Za-z0-9_]+)-V(?P<ver>[0-9_]+)-PKG(?P<pkg>[0-9_]+)(?:-(?P<build>[0-9_]+))?(?P<ext>\.zip)?$",
    re.IGNORECASE
)

def parse_package_filename_identity(filename_stem: str) -> Optional[Tuple[str, str, str]]:
    """Extract (Project_Name, Project_Version, Package_Version) from canonical filename."""
    match_result = PACKAGE_FILENAME_REGEX.match(filename_stem)
    if not match_result:
        return None
    
    project_name = match_result.group("name")
    raw_version = match_result.group("ver").replace("_", ".")
    raw_package = match_result.group("pkg").replace("_", "")
    
    return project_name, raw_version, raw_package

This parser operates seamlessly against incoming patterns like Management_CMS-V5.9.4-PKG128.zip, CLI_AI-V2134-PKG35.zip, and Project_Chunker-V180-PKG113.zip. If a match occurs, Tier 3 resolution automatically extracts metadata, eliminates manual prompt dialogs, and prepares the workspace for an atomic scoop.

4. The Zero-Data-Loss Atomic Scoop-and-Wipe (––scoop) Protocol

4.1 The Concept of Atomic Scoop-and-Wipe

During active software engineering, working directories and incoming drops rapidly clutter storage. Traditional archiving workflows rely on manual zip compression followed by unverified directory deletion. If the compression process fails midway, if permissions prevent full archival, or if bit rot occurs during disk write, the developer loses source code permanently.

The Project Chunker --scoop command eliminates this hazard entirely. It performs a verified, atomic capture-reconciliation-and-wipe pipeline. Source files are NEVER deleted until the serialized snapshot has been re-read from disk and reconciled byte-for-byte against the live filesystem.

4.2 Multi-Stage Execution Pipeline

+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                  The Atomic Scoop Verification Stage-Gate                |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  [Stage 1: Build Snapshot]                                               |
|    - Scan project root, compute streaming hashes, assemble matrix.       |
|    - Write atomic .tmp container to storage/project_snapshots/...        |
|    - Rename .tmp to canonical .bejson snapshot container.                |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                                     v
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  [Stage 2: Disk Write Flush & Manifest Reload]                           |
|    - Flush OS disk buffers (fsync).                                      |
|    - Completely reload and re-parse the snapshot .bejson from cold disk. |
|    - Compile O(1) Field Map Cache on re-read data.                       |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                                     v
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  [Stage 3: Live Byte-by-Byte Reconciliation]                             |
|    - For every entity row in re-read snapshot:                           |
|        1. Check file existence on live disk.                             |
|        2. Re-read live bytes from filesystem.                            |
|        3. Validate text/base64 payload parity against live bytes.        |
|        4. Re-calculate live SHA-256 and assert File_Hash equality.       |
|    - IF ANY DISCREPANCY DETECTED:                                        |
|        ===> HALT WITH FATAL ERROR. ZERO FILES UNLINKED.                  |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                     |
                                     v
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|  [Stage 4: Verified Unlinking & Parent Pruning]                          |
|    - Commit Master Registry and Project Tracker DB records.              |
|    - Unlink verified source files one-by-one.                            |
|    - Prune empty directory trees bottom-up.                              |
+--------------------------------------------------------------------------+

4.3 Live Byte-by-Byte Reconciliation Algorithm

The heart of the scoop safeguard is implemented in lib_bejson_Projects_verify.py. Below is the operational reconciliation loop that protects data integrity: 

def verify_snapshot_against_live_source(source_root: Path, snapshot_document: dict) -> bool:
    """Reconcile 100% of snapshot records against live disk bytes before unlinking."""
    field_map = {f["name"]: i for i, f in enumerate(snapshot_document["Fields"])}
    rel_idx = field_map["Relative_Path"]
    content_idx = field_map["File_Content"]
    b64_idx = field_map["Base64"]
    hash_idx = field_map["File_Hash"]
    flags_idx = field_map["Flags"]
    empty_idx = field_map["Is_Empty_Dir"]

    for row in snapshot_document["Values"]:
        rel_path = row[rel_idx]
        is_empty = row[empty_idx]
        live_target = source_root / rel_path

        if not live_target.exists():
            raise FileNotFoundError(f"Verification Failed: Missing live path {live_target}")

        if is_empty:
            if not live_target.is_dir():
                raise AssertionError(f"Expected empty dir at {live_target}")
            continue

        live_bytes = live_target.read_bytes()
        live_hash = hashlib.sha256(live_bytes).hexdigest()

        if live_hash != row[hash_idx]:
            raise ValueError(f"Hash Mismatch on {rel_path}: live={live_hash} snapshot={row[hash_idx]}")

        flags = json.loads(row[flags_idx]) if row[flags_idx] else []
        if "Is_Binary" in flags:
            expected_b64 = base64.b64encode(live_bytes).decode("ascii")
            if expected_b64 != row[b64_idx]:
                raise ValueError(f"Base64 corruption detected on binary file {rel_path}")
        else:
            expected_text = live_bytes.decode("utf-8")
            if expected_text != row[content_idx]:
                raise ValueError(f"Text content corruption detected on {rel_path}")

    return True  # 100% verified byte-for-byte parity

4.4 Failure Mitigation & Atomic Rollback Guarantees

Because Stage 3 executes strictly before Stage 4, any failure—whether caused by file locks, concurrent file modifications, permission denials, or disk hardware faults—triggers an immediate exception exit. The live directory remains 100% intact, and the generated snapshot container is retained in storage/project_snapshots/ for diagnostic inspection. No source file is ever deleted in an unverified state.

5. Restoration Pipelines, Archive Intake & Storage Integrity Auditing

5.1 Byte-Perfect Project Restoration Pipeline (--restore <UUID>)

Re-deploying an archived project back to the filesystem is executed via --restore <UUID> (or using an 8-character prefix match). The restoration pipeline executes the following deterministic phases:

  1. Registry Key Lookup: Queries storage/master/data/registry.bejson using an O(1) field map lookup on Versioned_UUID. Extracts the recorded Original_Path and Tracker_File.
  2. Destination Path Target: Sets the deployment target to Original_Path unless overridden via --dest <path>.
  3. Collision Guard: If destination files already exist on disk, the operation aborts unless --overwrite is explicitly supplied.
  4. Physical Reconstruction: Creates parent directories, restores empty directories (where Is_Empty_Dir=true), decodes Base64 payloads for binary files, and writes UTF-8 text for standard source files.
  5. Timestamp Restoration: Re-applies the recorded Modified_Time to every reconstructed file via os.utime, preserving compilation and cache timestamps.
  6. Tracker Re-Emission (--write-tracker): Extracts the verbatim bejson_project.json stored within the tracker database and writes it to the project root, returning the workspace to an immediately deployable state.

5.2 Automated Zip Intake & Anti-ZipSlip Security Auditing

Project Chunker natively processes .zip packages dropped into download folders. When a zip file is passed as the CLI target, the intake pipeline initiates an isolated extraction workflow protected by Anti-ZipSlip Security Auditing: 

def audit_and_safe_extract_zip(zip_archive_path: Path, staging_destination: Path) -> None:
    """Extract zip archive guarding against path traversal (ZipSlip) attacks."""
    canonical_staging_root = staging_destination.resolve()
    with zipfile.ZipFile(zip_archive_path, 'r') as archive:
        for member_info in archive.infolist():
            target_path = (staging_destination / member_info.filename).resolve()
            # Enforce strict path prefix boundary check
            if not str(target_path).startswith(str(canonical_staging_root) + os.sep):
                raise SecurityError(f"ZipSlip Traversal Blocked: {member_info.filename}")
        archive.extractall(staging_destination)

After safe unzipping, if the archive extracted to a single top-level parent folder, the engine transparently un-nests the project root. It then executes tracking, chunking, verified scooping of the temporary staging directory, and optionally removes the source zip archive (unless --keep-zip is supplied).

5.3 Deep Storage Integrity Verification (--verify)

Over months of storage on flash memory and SD cards, hardware storage media can suffer from silent bit rot. Project Chunker embeds an authoritative deep verification engine invoked via python3 CLI/project_chunker.py --verify:

  • Traverses every row in storage/master/data/registry.bejson.
  • Asserts that the referenced historical tracker file exists in storage/trackers/ and parses cleanly under BEJSON 104a.
  • Asserts that the physical snapshot container exists in storage/project_snapshots/.
  • Re-reads every entity record inside every snapshot, re-calculates the SHA-256 hash of every text and Base64 payload, and verifies parity against File_Hash.
  • Calculates and verifies the canonical Chunk_Digest.

5.4 Disaster Recovery & Registry Rebuilding from Snapshot Shards

If the Master Registry file (storage/master/data/registry.bejson) is accidentally deleted or corrupted, the system does not lose data. Because snapshot headers contain full provenance metadata (Project_Name, Project_Version, Package_Version, Versioned_UUID, Original_Path), the recovery utility crawls the storage/project_snapshots/ directory, parses the top-level headers of each snapshot file, and re-compiles the Master Registry from scratch with 100% mathematical fidelity.

5.5 Complete Python Implementation of the Restoration Engine

The restoration routine implemented in lib_bejson_Projects_restore.py reverses the snapshot container with strict validation. Below is the complete, annotated core loop that powers --restore: 

def execute_project_restoration(
    snapshot_data: dict,
    target_destination: Path,
    allow_overwrite: bool = False
) -> int:
    """Reconstruct directory tree and files with cryptographic fidelity."""
    target_destination = target_destination.resolve()
    target_destination.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    
    # Policy §6.2 O(1) Field Map Cache construction
    field_map = {fld["name"]: idx for idx, fld in enumerate(snapshot_data["Fields"])}
    rel_idx = field_map["Relative_Path"]
    content_idx = field_map["File_Content"]
    b64_idx = field_map["Base64"]
    flags_idx = field_map["Flags"]
    time_idx = field_map["Modified_Time"]
    empty_idx = field_map["Is_Empty_Dir"]

    restored_count = 0
    for entity_row in snapshot_data["Values"]:
        relative_path_string = entity_row[rel_idx]
        is_empty_directory = entity_row[empty_idx]
        destination_file_path = target_destination / relative_path_string

        # Guard against accidental overwrites
        if destination_file_path.exists() and not allow_overwrite:
            raise FileExistsError(f"Restoration halted: Destination exists: {destination_file_path}")

        # Ensure parent directory exists
        destination_file_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

        if is_empty_directory:
            destination_file_path.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
            restored_count += 1
            continue

        flags_list = json.loads(entity_row[flags_idx]) if entity_row[flags_idx] else []
        if "Is_Binary" in flags_list:
            raw_binary_bytes = base64.b64decode(entity_row[b64_idx].encode("ascii"))
            destination_file_path.write_bytes(raw_binary_bytes)
        else:
            destination_file_path.write_text(entity_row[content_idx], encoding="utf-8")

        # Restore original filesystem modification timestamp
        if entity_row[time_idx]:
            try:
                mtime_dt = datetime.fromisoformat(entity_row[time_idx])
                epoch_timestamp = mtime_dt.timestamp()
                os.utime(destination_file_path, (epoch_timestamp, epoch_timestamp))
            except Exception:
                pass

        restored_count += 1

    return restored_count

7. Best Practices, Policy Integration & Production Verification Checklist

7.1 Autonomous Agent Lifecycle Maintenance Integration

Project Chunker acts as the authoritative snapshot engine across Elton Boehnen's autonomous agent ecosystem. Per Policy Initialization Maintenance protocols:

  1. Session Initialization Sweeps: Incoming project packages in /storage/emulated/0/Download/ matching (NAME)-V(VER)-PKG(PKG) are swept and sorted. Duplicate intermediate builds are pruned, retaining the latest package in Download while archiving historical versions to $PROJECTS_ARCHIVE_ROOT/<type>/<project>/.
  2. Snapshotting Before Refactoring: Autonomous agents (Antigravity CLI, NewAgent) execute project_chunker.py --chunk "$SCRIPT_PATH" prior to executing large structural refactors, establishing an immutable baseline snapshot for rollback.
  3. Atomic Hand-Offs: Upon task completion, finished projects are registered via project_chunker.py --track "$SCRIPT_PATH" and committed to the daily log sink via python3 $LOGGING_TOOL write.

7.2 Solid Numeric Versioning & Changelog Discipline

To guarantee clean tracking across registries:

  • Solid Numeric Versioning (Policy §3.1): Version numbers should map to solid integers (e.g. 1.0.0 → 100). Package versions increment sequentially (+1 per delivery).
  • Changelog Hygiene (Policy §3.3): Every snapshot must maintain a continuously updated changelog in bejson_project.json. Re-delivering modified payloads under duplicate package versions is strictly prohibited.
  • Negative Constraints (Policy §7.3): AI assistants must never invent a Project_GUID or fabricate unlisted project types outside the Canonical Project Type Ledger (project_type_ledger.104a.bejson).
